Send a SCOUT First: Pre-hoc Reasoning for Adaptive Detector Allocation in Prompt-Injection Defense

Shuhao Zhang ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: UC San Diego Email: shz127@ucsd.edu    Jiarui Li11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign Email: q9cao@ucsd.edu    Qi Cao Affiliation: UC San Diego Email: ruz048@ucsd.edu    Ruiyi Zhang Affiliation: UC San Diego Email: p1xie@ucsd.edu    Pengtao Xie ††thanks: Correspondence to: Pengtao Xie <p1xie@ucsd.edu>. Affiliation: UC San Diego Email: jiarui27@illinois.edu
Abstract

Prompt-injection detectors are heterogeneous: each is strong on a different slice of attacks, and none is always reliable. Yet existing systems still treat detection as a fixed single-detector pipeline, committing every request to one detector’s blind spots. We reframe defense as detector allocation: given a heterogeneous pool, decide per request which detectors to run and whether to escalate to an LLM judge. Our framework SCOUT (Scalable and Controllable Outcome-prediction for Uncertainty-aware Triage) makes this decision dynamic by predicting each detector’s per-sample reliability and latency from how it behaved on similar past inputs, and exposes a single safety–utility threshold to the operator (where utility bundles benign-pass rate and wall-clock). To evaluate this setting, we build SCOUT-450, a benchmark that captures the structurally complex, agent-facing injections that older prompt-injection sets under-represent. On SCOUT-450, a safety-oriented operating point reduces attack-success rate by 𝟒𝟔%\mathbf{46\%} and total wall-clock by 𝟒𝟎%\mathbf{40\%} relative to an always-on GPT-4o judge, at a 5.1\mathbf{5.1}-point benign-utility drop. SCOUT also transfers to three external benchmarks (BIPIA, IPI, and IHEval), improving the safety–utility frontier.

1 Introduction

Large language models are increasingly deployed in systems that read external content such as tool outputs, retrieved documents, web pages, and emails. Instructions hidden in that content can hijack the model into ignoring its operator’s intent (Pérez and Ribeiro, 2022; Greshake et al., 2023). A practical production defense must balance safety (the fraction of attacks it catches) against utility (the per-request wall-clock and the pass-through rate for benign traffic).

Existing defenses sit at different points on the latency–accuracy spectrum: lexical rules, lightweight classifiers (ProtectAI, 2023; Li et al., 2025a), attention and hidden-state probes (Hung et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025), alignment-aware classifiers (Jia et al., 2026), and embedding or LLM-judge methods (Ganguly et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2023). The LLM judge, a frontier model such as GPT-4o prompted to read each request and return an attack/benign verdict, is the most accurate but by far the slowest: a single API call costs on the order of 1.51.5 s, about four orders of magnitude slower than a rule-based keyword and regex scanner that flags an input in well under a millisecond. These smaller, faster detectors are each strong on a different attack category, and on some of them one beats the judge (Section 7.2). Which detector is best therefore changes with the input, yet a standard cascade (Viola and Jones, 2001; Chen et al., 2024) fixes the order in advance and inherits the cheap detector’s mistakes wherever it is confident.

To address this, we propose SCOUT, which allocates detectors per input (Figure 2). Concretely, for each request SCOUT retrieves anchors with similar injection structure and reads how each detector behaved on them, and a small predictor then estimates which detectors are reliable for the input and how long each will take. The router runs the predicted-reliable light detectors in parallel, and escalates to an LLM judge only when their vote is uncertain. This makes SCOUT heterogeneity-aware: because the allocation is per input, each request can go to the detector that handles its attack category, including the categories where a small detector beats the judge. Two further properties follow from the same design. First, SCOUT is scalable, since adding a detector is just a single pass over the anchor set, with no retraining of the retriever, predictor, or routing rule. Second, SCOUT is controllable: a single operator threshold trades safety against latency, and because the predictor also estimates latency, the operator can fix this threshold to a latency budget before any request runs.

Our contributions are listed as follows:

  • •

    We reframe prompt-injection defense as per-input detector allocation. SCOUT chooses which detectors to trust for each request, so one deployment can match the detector to the input it faces.

  • •

    We propose SCOUT, which summarizes each detector’s past behavior as a fingerprint and trains a small predictor to estimate, for each input, which detectors are reliable and how long each takes. Allocating detectors from these estimates makes the defense tunable through one threshold with a predictable latency cost, and lets new detectors join with no retraining.

  • •

    We build SCOUT-450, a 450450-sample benchmark enriched for the structurally complex, agent-facing injections that older prompt-injection sets under-represent. On it, SCOUT lowers attack-success rate by 𝟒𝟔%\mathbf{46\%} and total wall-clock by 𝟒𝟎%\mathbf{40\%} against an always-on GPT-4o judge, at a 5.15.1-point benign-utility cost, and the same system transfers to BIPIA, IPI, and IHEval with no retraining.

2 Related Work

Prompt-injection attacks and benchmarks.

Research on prompt injection spans direct attacks (Pérez and Ribeiro, 2022) and indirect attacks embedded in external content (Greshake et al., 2023), with taxonomies and benchmarks that define the attack space, instruction hierarchy, and agent-facing settings (Liu et al., 2024b; Wallace et al., 2024; Yi et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025c; Liu et al., 2025a) and analyze how instruction placement and transferable patterns shape vulnerability (Li et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025b).

Defenses.

Standalone defenses span lexical guards and trained classifiers (ProtectAI, 2023; Chen et al., 2025a; Li et al., 2025a; Jacob et al., 2025), attention and hidden-state probes (Hung et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2025), alignment-aware classifiers (Jia et al., 2026; Min et al., 2026), embedding-OOD (Ganguly et al., 2026) and semantic-intent detectors (Wang et al., 2025), prompt-modification techniques (Chen et al., 2025b; Zhang et al., 2025a), and LLM judges (Zheng et al., 2023), each fixing its own safety, utility, and latency trade-off. Cascades escalate from cheap to expensive stages (Viola and Jones, 2001; Chen et al., 2024), and composed systems combine components through a rule fixed at design time (Le et al., 2026; Hossain et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025b). All commit to a routing rule before seeing the input.

Routing and pre-hoc outcome prediction.

Outside prompt injection, cascades (Viola and Jones, 2001) and selective prediction (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017) defer hard cases to a stronger model when confidence is low; FrugalGPT (Chen et al., 2024) and RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2024) route among LLM tiers; and SCOPE (Cao et al., 2026) predicts per-model outcome and cost from behavioral fingerprints. Ball et al. (2025) prove cryptographic impossibility results for input filters weaker than the target LLM.

3 Detector Fingerprints and Retrieval

Let x=(policy,goal,eval_content)x=(\text{policy},\text{goal},\text{eval\_content}) denote an input request and 𝒟={D1,…,DM}\mathcal{D}=\{D_{1},\dots,D_{M}\} the available detector pool, where each detector DD produces a binary verdict y^D​(x)∈{0,1}\hat{y}_{D}(x)\in\{0,1\} (1 = attack) at wall-clock ℓD​(x)∈ℝ+\ell_{D}(x)\in\mathbb{R}_{+}. We partition 𝒟\mathcal{D} into a light pool 𝒟light\mathcal{D}_{\text{light}} that the routing layer can invoke in parallel and a single LLM judge DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} (indexed D6D_{6}) reserved for escalation. SCOUT exposes an operator-facing threshold τ\tau (Section 5) that controls how often the router escalates to the judge, trading wall-clock for safety and benign utility.

Safety–utility evaluation axes.

We report four quantities. Safety is the attack-success rate (ASR=FN/Natk\mathrm{ASR}=\mathrm{FN}/N_{\mathrm{atk}}, lower is safer). Utility combines benign utility (BU=1−FPR\mathrm{BU}=1-\mathrm{FPR}) and total wall-clock latency over the benchmark. Accuracy (Acc\mathrm{Acc}) is the class-balanced summary of 1−ASR1-\mathrm{ASR} and BU\mathrm{BU}, reported alongside the two axes. Sweeping τ\tau traces the safety–utility trade-off.

Detector fingerprints.

To characterize detectors without retraining the router, we fix an anchor set 𝒜={ai}i=1N𝒜\mathcal{A}=\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathcal{A}}} of representative inputs (Section 6). For any detector DD, we record its behavior on every anchor to form a detector fingerprint

ϕ𝒜​(D)={(ai,y^D​(ai),ℓD​(ai))}i=1N𝒜,\phi_{\mathcal{A}}(D)\;=\;\bigl\{\,(a_{i},\;\hat{y}_{D}(a_{i}),\;\ell_{D}(a_{i}))\,\bigr\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathcal{A}}}, (1)

where y^D​(ai)∈{0,1}\hat{y}_{D}(a_{i})\in\{0,1\} is the verdict and ℓD​(ai)∈ℝ+\ell_{D}(a_{i})\in\mathbb{R}_{+} the latency. An off-the-shelf LLM (GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI, 2025a)) serializes each entry into a short structured record stating a one-sentence detector profile, the anchor’s category and carrier, and DD’s observed verdict, correctness, and latency. This makes detector integration training-free: adding a detector requires only a single pass over 𝒜\mathcal{A} to generate its fingerprint, with no gradient update to the retriever, predictor, or router.

Retrieval-augmented context.

At inference, for a test input xx we retrieve the most relevant anchors by dense retrieval (Karpukhin et al., 2020). Let s⁡(x,a)s(x,a) be the cosine similarity between the asymmetric embeddings of xx and an anchor aa; we retrieve the top-KK anchors

𝒜K​(x)=Top​-​Ka∈𝒜⁡s⁡(x,a),\mathcal{A}_{K}(x)\;=\;\mathop{\mathrm{Top\text{-}}K}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\;s(x,a), (2)

where the embedder is instructed to align on injection structure: category, hiding strategy, carrier, and attack mechanism. Topical content is ignored. Retrieval is detector-agnostic, so the single ranking 𝒜K​(x)\mathcal{A}_{K}(x) serves the whole pool. The retrieved fingerprint slice serves two purposes: it is serialized into the conditioning context of the outcome predictor (Section 4), and the empirical accuracy of each detector over 𝒜K​(x)\mathcal{A}_{K}(x) defines a per-sample trust prior πx,D∈[0,1]\pi_{x,D}\in[0,1] used by the triage rule (Section 5). Retrieval instructions and the trust-prior definition are in Appendix C.

4 Outcome Predictor

The predictor is a small language model that estimates, for each (sample, detector) pair (x,D)(x,D), whether DD will be correct on xx and how long it will run. Its target is detector correctness 𝟏[y^D(x)=y(x)]\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{D}(x)=y(x)], which the router then aggregates across the pool. Conditioned on a prompt P⁡(x,D)P(x,D) that concatenates the detector profile, the retrieved fingerprint records (Section 3), and the target sample, it samples

z,(pred_corr,pred_lat)∼pθ(⋅|P(x,D))z,(\texttt{pred\_corr},\texttt{pred\_lat})\,\sim\,p_{\theta}(\,\cdot\,|\,P(x,D)) (3)

where zz is a short reasoning chain and (pred_corr,pred_lat)∈{0,1}×ℝ+(\texttt{pred\_corr},\texttt{pred\_lat})\in\{0,1\}\times\mathbb{R}_{+} is the structured prediction. Because the prompt carries the detector’s text profile, one set of parameters θ\theta serves every detector in the pool. We instantiate pθp_{\theta} as Qwen3-4B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025) with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022), trained on SCOUT-30K (Section 6) in two stages.

Stage 1: SFT via hindsight distillation.

Following Cao et al. (2026), we warm-start θ\theta by supervised fine-tuning on hindsight-distilled rationales (Liu et al., 2024a): a teacher sees the prompt, the detector verdict y^D​(x)\hat{y}_{D}(x), the gold label y⁡(x)y(x), and latency ℓD​(x)\ell_{D}(x), then writes a concise zz that justifies the target (𝟏[y^D(x)=y(x)],ℓD(x))(\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{D}(x)=y(x)],\ell_{D}(x)). The predictor learns to emit (z,pred_corr,pred_lat)(z,\texttt{pred\_corr},\texttt{pred\_lat}), which fixes the output format and bounds length.

Stage 2: GRPO.

On top of the chain-of-thought SFT variant, we align the predictor using group-relative policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024) with a gated multiplicative reward

R⁡(o,x,D)=gfmt​(o)⋅rcorr​(o)⋅(1+rlat​(o)),R(o;x,D)\;=\;g_{\text{fmt}}(o)\cdot r_{\text{corr}}(o)\cdot\bigl(1+r_{\text{lat}}(o)\bigr), (4)

where gfmtg_{\text{fmt}} is a format gate, rcorrr_{\text{corr}} matches pred_corr to 𝟏[y^D(x)=y(x)]\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{D}(x)=y(x)], and rlatr_{\text{lat}} rewards an accurate latency estimate. The multiplicative form keeps correctness dominant: a wrong correctness prediction zeros the reward whatever the latency. The training corpus, the chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022) variants used in the ablations, the full reward, the GRPO objective, and the hyperparameters are in Appendix D.

5 Uncertainty-Aware Triage

Algorithm 1 turns the predictor’s per-detector estimates into a per-sample allocation. A subset selector keeps the light detectors the predictor marks reliable on xx; they run in parallel and cast a trust-weighted vote. When the vote’s agreement falls below τ\tau, an escalation gate consults the LLM judge, but only when the predictor also marks the judge reliable on xx; otherwise the subset vote stands. Because the predictor also estimates each detector’s latency, the rule returns the predicted wall-clock ℓ^​(x)\hat{\ell}(x) of the path taken, which makes τ\tau a latency control (Section 7.6). Appendix E details the trust weighting, the empty-subset fallback, and the symmetric escalation gate, and Section 7.3 ablates the selector and the gate separately.

Since ℓ^​(x)\hat{\ell}(x) never enters the routing decision, summing it over the stream yields the total wall-clock T^​(τ)=∑xℓ^​(x)\hat{T}(\tau)=\sum_{x}\hat{\ell}(x) that SCOUT predicts for any τ\tau before running. The operator can therefore meet a latency budget LL without labels by selecting

τ∗​(L)=max⁡{τ:T^​(τ)≤L},\tau^{*}(L)=\max\{\tau:\hat{T}(\tau)\leq L\}, (5)

the safest threshold within budget. The trust-mixing weight ω∈[0,1]\omega\in[0,1] balances the per-sample and global trust priors. Appendix E gives the budget-to-τ\tau recipes and the operating point we report, and Appendix F sweeps ω\omega.

6 Data

We use four mutually disjoint data roles. An upstream prompt-injection corpus (BIPIA (Yi et al., 2025) and related public sets) trains our D2D_{2}, D3D_{3}, D5D_{5}, D7D_{7}, and D8D_{8} detectors. The SCOUT-specific data consist of SCOUT-30K, with 29,55129{,}551 hindsight-distilled (sample, detector) examples for predictor supervision; Anchor-400, a 400400-sample fingerprint set for kNN retrieval and trust priors; and SCOUT-450, a 450450-sample evaluation benchmark (255255 attack / 195195 benign) intentionally enriched for the harder hidden_tricky category. Appendix B gives the construction, sampling, and composition of each split.

7 Experiments

We organize the experiments around four research questions:

  • •

    RQ1. Does SCOUT improve the safety–utility trade-off over standalone detectors and the always-on DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}?

  • •

    RQ2. Which design choice produces the gain?

  • •

    RQ3. Can SCOUT absorb new detectors and a swapped LLM judge without retraining?

  • •

    RQ4. Does the framework transfer to benchmarks it was not trained on?

7.1 Setup

Detector pool.

The pool spans six detector families: lexical and structural rules (D1D_{1}); lightweight ML classifiers over sentence embeddings (D2D_{2}, seven variants); a fine-tuned DeBERTa-v3 classifier (D3D_{3}) (He et al., 2023; ProtectAI, 2023); an attention-based diagnostic (D4D_{4}) (Hung et al., 2025); an alignment-aware classifier (D5D_{5}) (Jia et al., 2026); and an LLM-as-judge (DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}) (Zheng et al., 2023). The default light pool is {D1,D2KNN,D2LR,D2XGB,D3,D4,D5}\{D_{1},D_{2}^{\text{KNN}},D_{2}^{\text{LR}},D_{2}^{\text{XGB}},D_{3},D_{4},D_{5}\}, which the router runs in parallel, with GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) as the escalation judge DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}. Per-detector backbones and training corpora are in Appendix A.

Protocol.

RQ1–RQ3 use the held-out SCOUT-450 benchmark and RQ4 the external BIPIA, IPI, and IHEval benchmarks. Unless noted, SCOUT runs the SFT++GRPO predictor over this light pool with trust mixing ω=0.6\omega=0.6. We compare SCOUT against the individual standalone detectors and the always-on DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}; alternative routing rules and predictors are ablations of SCOUT introduced in Section 7.3. Metrics follow Section 3; Appendix K gives the serving stack and latency model.

7.2 Safety–utility frontier on SCOUT-450 (RQ1)

On SCOUT-450, per-input allocation improves the safety–utility trade-off over every single-detector baseline in Table 1, including the judge DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} (GPT-4o) run on every request. At the headline operating point, SCOUT records the lowest Total ASR (.063.063) and the highest accuracy (.933.933): it is safer than the safest single detector (PIGuard, .098.098) and more accurate than the most accurate one (DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}, .924.924), at about 0.6×0.6\times the wall-clock of DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}. No single detector reaches both corners at once. The only axis on which DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} leads is benign utility (.979.979 vs. .928.928), the throughput that τ\tau trades for safety.

The threshold τ\tau exposes a usable control surface across this frontier: low-τ\tau points stay on the light pool and finish in a fraction of the headline wall-clock, while raising τ\tau spends judge calls to tighten safety, so an operator reads off the point that meets its budget. Across the sweep SCOUT’s curve sits above the individual-detector points on every quality axis and to the left of the DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} marker (Figure 3).

The gain comes from detector heterogeneity. No single detector is strong everywhere, so a fixed deployment inherits one detector’s profile across the whole stream. For each input, SCOUT predicts which light detectors are reliable and runs only those, escalating to the judge only when their vote is uncertain. The routed system therefore stays at or near the best detector in every attack category at once (Table 1), giving it an aggregate ASR below any fixed choice.

7.3 Where the gain comes from (RQ2)

RQ2 asks why the frontier improves. Table 2 changes one link of SCOUT at a time (the reliability predictor, the allocation rule, or the trust mixing) while keeping the rest fixed, except that predictor-recipe rows use their own best τ\tau; Figure 4 shows the same three axes as threshold-swept attack-block-rate curves.

Predictor quality determines whether SCOUT can exploit detector heterogeneity. Replacing only the reliability estimator weakens the routed system: attack leakage rises from .063.063 ASR to .086.086–.110.110 for the alternatives. The predictor estimates each detector’s predicted correctness for the current input, and the routing gain comes mainly from calibrating this estimate on the light pool. Appendix H traces it to two learned behaviors: the SFT++GRPO predictor is both more accurate and more concise than the SFT, zero-shot, and non-LLM (KNN, MLP) variants, and removing the reasoning chain lowers predicted-correctness accuracy.

Per-input allocation matters beyond ensembling. Using the same detector pool, the no-predictor cascade and the uniform-trust cascade both leave more attacks unblocked (.090.090 and .078.078 ASR, versus .063.063 for SCOUT): the former lets detectors vote where fingerprints mark them unreliable, and the latter gives a category specialist and a noisy detector equal weight. SCOUT separates these roles, with the selector setting membership and the trust prior setting vote mass (Appendix E). In Figure 4, at matched wall-clock its predictor-filtered cascade sits above both cascades on attack block rate while tracking them on BU, so the gain comes from allocation rather than from trading BU for ASR.

Trust mixing stabilizes local fingerprint evidence. Both endpoints hurt: ω=0\omega=0 ignores the retrieved neighborhood, and ω=1\omega=1 overweights a small one and raises ASR to .075.075. The middle range is best; we use ω=0.6\omega=0.6, and Appendix F gives the full sweep.

7.4 Pool reconfiguration exposes controllable operating points (RQ3)

RQ3 tests whether SCOUT can absorb pool changes after training. A router tied to detector IDs or a fixed cascade would need new labels or calibration when the judge or light detectors change; SCOUT takes in a new component from its behavior on the anchor set alone. We freeze the trained predictor, retriever, routing rule, trust mixing, and threshold τ\tau, and let each new judge or light detector enter only through a detector fingerprint built from one pass over Anchor-400, with no fine-tuning, calibration fit, or gradient update. Table 3 applies this protocol on SCOUT-450.

The Base rows swap the LLM judge while keeping the light pool fixed, testing whether the judge is a hard-coded endpoint or another fingerprinted component. The extension rows add D7D_{7} (DistilBERT) and D8D_{8} (InstructDetector), absent from the Base light pool (Appendix A). These added detectors do not monotonically improve every metric; they expose different safety, benign-utility, and latency points under the same decision rule: with GPT-4o, adding D8D_{8} raises BU from .928.928 to .949.949 while increasing ASR from .063.063 to .102.102. This is the intended behavior of detector allocation: pool composition changes the set of available detector behaviors, while τ\tau controls how conservatively SCOUT escalates beyond them.

7.5 Cross-benchmark generalization (RQ4)

RQ4 stress-tests SCOUT under distribution shift across BIPIA, IPI, and IHEval. IPI and IHEval are fully external, used in no part of SCOUT; BIPIA feeds SCOUT-30K and SCOUT-450, so the BIPIA slice evaluated here is de-intersected from those splits and from detector training, disjoint from everything SCOUT saw (Appendix J). We run the SCOUT-450-selected configuration unchanged on all three, with no benchmark-specific calibration.

Table 4 reports the six benchmark–judge cells. SCOUT cuts wall-clock in all of them and lowers ASR in five, with the largest safety margin on BIPIA; on IPI it stays close to the already-strong judge on accuracy while blocking more attacks. The strongest light detector changes across benchmarks, and on BIPIA it outperforms the judge (Table 8), so the transfer comes from re-allocating detectors per benchmark.

IHEval differs in attack form: it pits instructions at different hierarchy levels against each other. Most light detectors fall near chance here, and only D4D_{4} (degenerate on BIPIA and IPI) carries signal, so SCOUT escalates more and its safety gain narrows. Under GPT-4o it gives up the judge’s near-complete attack recall (the lone ASR regression) for substantially higher benign utility and accuracy at far lower wall-clock.

7.6 Latency and deployment discussion

Two points carry the deployment story; Appendix K gives the full model, the per-predictor breakdown, and the break-even derivation.

τ\tau dials wall-clock, predictably. Because SCOUT predicts each detector’s latency, it predicts the wall-clock of its own routing, and the predicted total T^​(τ)\hat{T}(\tau) follows the realized cost across the τ\tau-sweep (in-distribution gap 2.5%2.5\%, and the same monotone trend transfers to the external benchmarks; Appendix K, Figure 23). An operator therefore sets latency by choosing τ\tau against a predicted budget, with no live measurement: the budget-to-τ\tau map (Appendix E, Figure 17) sends a target latency budget (or a safety budget) to the threshold τ⋆\tau^{\star} that meets it, label-free for the latency budget since T^​(τ)\hat{T}(\tau) comes from pred_lat.

Where the budget goes. At the headline point SCOUT spends 395395 s versus 656656 s for the always-on GPT-4o judge (Table 1), and the saving comes entirely from requests that finish on the filtered light pool. The judge call remains the largest cost term, so τ\tau moves wall-clock mainly through the escalation rate, which rises with τ\tau while the light-pool mix stays roughly constant (Appendix E, Figure 18); the per-path breakdown and the predictor’s own (small) overhead are in Appendix K.

8 Conclusion

We reframe prompt-injection defense as detector allocation: the system decides per input which detectors to trust, combining behavioral fingerprints, a small predictor that estimates each detector’s per-input reliability and latency, and an uncertainty-gated routing rule. Because the predictor also estimates latency, a single operator threshold tunes the safety–latency trade-off against a budget known before any request runs, and a new detector joins through one anchor-set pass with no retraining. On SCOUT-450 and three external benchmarks (BIPIA, IPI, IHEval), SCOUT improves the safety–utility trade-off over every single-detector baseline, including the always-on DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}.

Looking forward, we will release the predictor checkpoint, the SCOUT-30K training set, and the SCOUT-450 and Anchor-400 splits, and we maintain the detector fingerprint library so operators can assemble their own detector pools. We will also open-source the full pipeline soon.

Limitations

Dependence on the available pool. SCOUT composes detectors; it does not improve any single detector. If the candidate pool contains no detector with usable signal on the target distribution, the routed system cannot exceed what the pool can support; its operating point on the safety–utility frontier is bounded by what the pool can collectively achieve.

Anchor coverage and evaluation scope. The trust prior and the predictor’s retrieved context are useful in proportion to how well Anchor-400 covers the test distribution along the structural axes the embedder targets (category, hiding strategy, carrier, attack mechanism); when a test input falls far from every anchor, the per-sample component of the effective trust becomes noisier and the router leans more on the precomputed global prior π¯D\bar{\pi}_{D} (diagnostics in Appendix C). Our benchmarks (SCOUT-450, BIPIA, IPI, IHEval) are also English-only and centered on a fixed taxonomy of prompt-injection mechanisms, so we do not evaluate cross-lingual transfer or attacks outside this taxonomy. Either shift would require refreshing the anchor set to reflect the new structural axes, which is a one-pass operation per detector. SCOUT-450 is also a compact, fully hand-curated diagnostic benchmark (450450 samples); we keep it small to guarantee per-sample category, carrier, and difficulty labels for fine-grained attribution, and our generalization claims rest on the three external benchmarks.

Setup-dependent latency and adaptive attacks. Absolute wall-clock numbers depend on our A100 + vLLM serving stack and on the median per-detector accounting used in Appendix K, and the reported predictor uses a single SFT++GRPO recipe over Qwen3-4B-Instruct whose light-pool calibration is the lever behind most of the routing gain (Section 7.3); other stacks or predictor backbones should re-measure. We also do not study adaptive attackers that target the router itself, for example by crafting samples that flip the predictor’s estimate for DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} to suppress a useful escalation.

Appendix A Detector pool details

The detector pool 𝒟\mathcal{D} comprises a base pool of six families used throughout the main-text experiments (D1D_{1}–D5D_{5} plus DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}), two additional detectors used in the pool-reconfiguration study (D7D_{7}, D8D_{8}), and one further single-detector baseline reported for reference but not integrated into SCOUT’s pool (D9D_{9}).

Base pool.

  • •

    D1D_{1}: Lexical / structural rules (training-free; CPU-only; sub-millisecond latency). A keyword and regex screen for explicit injection markers (ignore the above, new instruction, override, etc.), suspicious tags (⟨|\langle\!|im_start|⟩|\!\rangle and variants), structural anomalies (e.g. HTML comments inside benign content), and base64/hex/unicode-escape patterns indicating obfuscation. The rule list is hand-curated from prior threat reports and does not learn from data.

  • •

    D2D_{2}: Lightweight ML classifiers over sentence embeddings (trainable; CPU/GPU; ~10 ms). Seven variants share the same input pipeline: a fixed sentence embedding (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019) (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025b)) of the request content is fed to one of {logistic regression, linear SVM, RBF SVM, XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016), kk-nearest neighbors over the embedding (k=25k{=}25), MLP, random forest}. All variants are trained on the upstream corpus described below and never updated after deployment. We report D2LRD_{2}^{\text{LR}}, D2XGBD_{2}^{\text{XGB}}, and D2KNND_{2}^{\text{KNN}} separately in the per-detector tables.

  • •

    D3D_{3}: Fine-tuned transformer classifier (trainable; GPU; ~10 ms). DeBERTa-v3-base (∼\sim184M parameters) (He et al., 2023; ProtectAI, 2023) fine-tuned end-to-end on our detector training set with binary cross-entropy.

  • •

    D4D_{4}: Attention-based diagnostic (training-free; GPU; ~18 ms). Implements Attention Tracker (Hung et al., 2025) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Llama Team, 2024): a single forward pass measures the ratio of attention mass placed on the operator’s goal tokens vs. the document tokens; samples below a fixed ratio threshold are flagged as injections. The detector is highly sensitive to long carriers and tends to flag legitimate tool outputs, which is reflected in its degenerate benign utility on SCOUT-450.

  • •

    D5D_{5}: Alignment-aware classifier (trainable; GPU; ~60 ms). AlignSentinel (Jia et al., 2026): an MLP probe we train on our detector training set over a frozen instruction-tuned LLM’s attention features, producing a three-way classification (attack, aligned instruction, benign). We collapse the two non-attack labels into a binary attack/benign verdict.

  • •

    DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}: LLM-as-judge (training-free; API; ~1.5 s). Prompts an off-the-shelf instruction-tuned LLM (Zheng et al., 2023) to read the request and produce a binary attack/benign verdict with a short rationale. The main-text experiments use GPT-4o as DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}; the candidates we considered and the selection protocol are reported in Appendix L.

Pool extensions (RQ3).

  • •

    D7D_{7}: Lightweight indirect-injection classifier (trainable; GPU; ~6 ms). A DistilBERT-base classifier (Sanh et al., 2019) from the indirect-injection detection study of Chen et al. (2025a), fine-tuned to detect injected instructions in retrieved external content. We train it on our detector training set and add it to the light pool in the D7D_{7} extension row of Table 3.

  • •

    D8D_{8}: Instruction-tuned hidden-state probe (trainable; GPU; ~60 ms). InstructDetector (Wen et al., 2025), a probe over the internal hidden states of an instruction-tuned LLM, trained on our detector training set to identify task hijacking. Added to the light pool in the D7+D8D_{7}{+}D_{8} extension row.

Single-detector baseline (not in any SCOUT pool).

  • •

    D9D_{9}: PIGuard prompt guard (trainable; GPU; ~450 ms). PIGuard (Li et al., 2025a) is a DeBERTa-derived prompt guard with the Mitigating Over-defense for Free training procedure, designed to suppress trigger-word bias. We use the released PIGuard model and report its standalone metrics on SCOUT-450 and the three external benchmarks as a single-detector reference. PIGuard appears only as a standalone baseline, outside the SCOUT light pool.

Upstream corpus for trainable detectors.

The D2D_{2} family, D3D_{3}, D5D_{5}, D7D_{7}, and D8D_{8} are trained on our detector training set, a prompt-injection corpus assembled from BIPIA (Yi et al., 2025) and adjacent public datasets; D9D_{9} is the released PIGuard model. This corpus is dominated by short, structurally simple carriers and a relatively narrow attack-template distribution. Parts of BIPIA also seed portions of SCOUT-30K and a small portion of SCOUT-450. The BIPIA subset we evaluate on as an external benchmark (Section 7.5, Table 4) is a separate, de-duplicated 1,0001{,}000-sample slice disjoint from every BIPIA example used in detector training, SCOUT-30K, and SCOUT-450, so the cross-benchmark numbers carry no training overlap.

The per-detector single-classifier metrics on SCOUT-450 are read off the standalone rows of Table 1; the external-benchmark per-detector breakdown is in Table 8.

Detector behavioral diversity.

Figure 5 compares the standalone detectors by median per-request latency and accuracy on SCOUT-30K and SCOUT-450. The pool spans four orders of magnitude in latency, from the sub-millisecond rule scanner to the second-scale LLM judge. The judge is the most accurate (about .93.93) and by far the slowest; every light detector is one to four orders of magnitude faster, at lower and uneven accuracy. Each detector’s latency and accuracy is stable across the two splits, so the per-detector behavior the predictor learns on SCOUT-30K transfers to SCOUT-450. The per-category breakdown behind these aggregates is in Table 1: no detector dominates across categories, and the judge is not a strict superset of the light pool, since some inputs are caught only by a light detector.

Per-detector correctness on the sample space.

Figure 6 projects SCOUT-450 samples onto a shared UMAP (the same layout shown by metadata in Figure 9) and overlays each detector’s correctness pattern, with errors split into false positives and false negatives. Green dots mark samples the detector classifies correctly, dark-blue crosses mark false positives, and orange crosses mark false negatives. The overlay shows that error regions differ qualitatively across detectors: D1D_{1} and the D2D_{2} family miss attacks (false negatives) on long structured carriers, D4D_{4} raises false positives across dense benign regions, D5D_{5} misses inputs concentrated on the right-side hidden_tricky cluster, and the LLM judge has a smaller, more scattered error set. These per-detector error geometries are what the predictor exploits when it filters the light pool per input.

Detector error atlas.

Figure 7 expands the standalone SCOUT-450 view from category-level accuracy to a per-sample error atlas. Columns are detectors and rows are category-grouped samples; each cell marks whether that detector is correct, produces a false positive, or misses an attack. The atlas shows that errors are concentrated but not identical across detectors, with the densest false-negative region on hidden_tricky. This per-sample heterogeneity gives the router useful choices, since no single detector is best everywhere.

Appendix B Data construction and composition

The data pipeline has four roles, summarized in Section 6. Figure 8 shows the attack/benign and per-category composition of the three released SCOUT splits. The SCOUT splits are mutually disjoint. Trainable-detector weights are learned outside this paper; the detector-training examples and the evaluated BIPIA slice are de-duplicated against SCOUT-30K, Anchor-400, and SCOUT-450.

Attack categories.

SCOUT-450 and the SCOUT-30K source carriers are annotated along two orthogonal axes: an attack category (six values, including two benign) describing the high-level intent of the request, and a carrier type (thirteen values) describing the surface form in which that intent is delivered. The taxonomy extends the indirect-injection categories of BIPIA (Yi et al., 2025) and the indirect-injection detection benchmark of Chen et al. (2025a) with explicit benign-but-adversarially-styled controls (aligned_instruction) and a hardened-against-detectors category (hidden_tricky). The six attack categories are:

  • •

    hidden_tricky (hid; 146146 on SCOUT-450). Attacks whose injected instruction is embedded in a structurally complex carrier (long HTML, tool output, emails with quoted threads, code with comments) such that it is plausibly legitimate at the surface level. This is the deliberately hardest category and the largest single bucket in SCOUT-450; it is where existing single detectors are weakest.

  • •

    tool_misuse (tool; 4242). Attacks that abuse the operator’s available tool calls, either by smuggling tool-call instructions inside retrieved content or by directing the model to call a tool with attacker-controlled arguments. Modeled on the tool-misuse threat in Wen et al. (2025) and the agent-facing settings of Liu et al. (2025a).

  • •

    exfiltration (exf; 4141). Attacks that ask the model to leak information from the system prompt, prior conversation, or retrieved context to the attacker (e.g. by emitting it verbatim or by encoding it into a URL). Aligned with the data-exfiltration category in BIPIA (Yi et al., 2025).

  • •

    direct_misaligned (dir; 2626). Direct prompt injection in the original sense of Pérez and Ribeiro (2022): the injected instruction explicitly overrides the operator’s stated goal (e.g. “ignore the above and instead…”), with no obfuscation.

  • •

    totally_benign (benign; 9090). Benign requests with no instruction-following content beyond the operator’s stated goal. Includes plain factual queries, summarization requests, and benign tool outputs.

  • •

    aligned_instruction (aligned; 105105). Benign requests whose content contains imperative language or instruction-shaped fragments that align with the operator’s goal (e.g. a summarization request whose source document itself contains instructions for a third party). This category controls for high-recall detectors that conflate benign instructions with injection attempts.

The first four categories together form the attack subset (N=255N{=}255); the last two form the benign subset (N=195N{=}195).

Carrier types.

The carrier type records the surface form of the request content. The thirteen values used in SCOUT-450 are: tool_output (106106), plain_text (6666), code (4545), email (4343), tool_description (4040), html (3939), markdown (2727), table (2626), encoding_obfuscation (2323), qa_context (2020), chat_transcript (99), agent_memory (44), browser_trace (22). The carrier list is drawn from common LLM-tool integrations and reflects the surface forms exercised in agent benchmarks (Liu et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2025c). encoding_obfuscation covers base64, hex, and unicode-escape wrappings of attack payloads. The category and carrier axes are independent: any attack category can appear in any carrier type, and SCOUT-450 samples are stratified to populate the (category, carrier) cross-product where natural examples exist.

Annotation procedure.

The SCOUT splits were constructed and labeled in-house by the authors. Candidate samples were generated programmatically from carrier templates and then reviewed by the authors for the binary attack/benign label, the attack category, and the carrier type; SCOUT-450 was further hand-curated to over-sample the harder hidden_tricky category. We did not use crowdworkers, paid annotators, or any external human-subjects pipeline, so no recruitment, payment, consent, or ethics-board protocol applies.

Personally identifying information and offensive content.

All SCOUT samples are synthetic. Carriers contain fictional entities (company names, account identifiers, API keys) generated for the templates, with no real-person personally identifying information. The attack content consists of standard prompt-injection patterns (instruction override, credential exfiltration, task hijacking) of the same kind found in the public benchmarks we compare against; it contains no hateful, harassing, or otherwise offensive material beyond the prompt-injection threat model itself. We therefore did not apply additional anonymization beyond using synthetic identifiers.

SCOUT-30K, predictor supervision.

SCOUT-30K initializes the predictor (Section 4). We start from 2,7002{,}700 source carriers spanning the same six prompt-injection categories and thirteen carrier types as SCOUT-450. For each (carrier, detector) pair, a teacher produces a rationale and structured prediction (pred_corr, pred_lat). We keep only pairs whose teacher prediction matches the target (𝟏[y^D(x)=y(x)],ℓD(x))(\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{D}(x)=y(x)],\ell_{D}(x)), yielding 29,55129{,}551 ShareGPT-format hindsight-distillation examples across all detectors in 𝒟\mathcal{D}. The category and carrier marginals (Figure 8a) mirror SCOUT-450, so predictor training matches the evaluation distribution at the split level.

Anchor-400, fingerprint set.

Anchor-400 is a held-out 400400-sample set used to populate the fingerprint database (Section 3). Its category and carrier mix (Figure 8b) mirrors the source carriers used for SCOUT-30K, but its samples are disjoint from both SCOUT-30K and SCOUT-450. Each detector in 𝒟\mathcal{D} is run once on every anchor. The resulting (y^D​(a),ℓD​(a))(\hat{y}_{D}(a),\ell_{D}(a)) pairs, a one-sentence detector profile, and a brief sample description form the per-(anchor, detector) fingerprint record. Anchor-400 is used for fingerprint construction, kNN retrieval, and the trust prior; it is not predictor-training data and is not part of the evaluation benchmark.

SCOUT-450, evaluation benchmark.

SCOUT-450 is the 450450-sample held-out evaluation set used throughout the paper. It contains 255255 attack and 195195 benign samples. We intentionally over-sample hidden_tricky (146146 samples), which covers long, structurally complex carriers such as HTML pages, emails, code blocks, and tool outputs with adversarial fragments interleaved among legitimate content. This is where existing single detectors are weakest and where routing should matter most. Figure 8c gives the per-category and per-carrier counts. SCOUT-450 is disjoint from SCOUT-30K and Anchor-400, so evaluation samples are unseen by both predictor training and fingerprint construction.

Sample space by metadata.

Figure 9 lays out the SCOUT-450 eval_content embeddings on a shared UMAP, colored by attack category, carrier type, and difficulty. Samples organize by injection structure: the long structured carriers (HTML, email, tool output) form the lower-right filament, and hidden_tricky concentrates on the right. The per-detector correctness overlay in Appendix A (Figure 6) reuses this exact layout.

Sample difficulty.

Figure 10 scores each SCOUT-450 sample by how many of the eight base-pool detectors (D1D_{1}, the three D2D_{2} variants, D3D_{3}, D4D_{4}, D5D_{5}, and the GPT-4o judge) misclassify it. The count spans the full range from 00 to 88: most samples are missed by one to three detectors, a tail is missed by six or more, and the hardest samples concentrate in hidden_tricky. These counts make SCOUT-450 a direct test of routing across easy and hard inputs.

Anchor coverage of the predictor training distribution.

Anchor-400 supplies the fixed reference set for the kNN trust prior and the predictor’s retrieved context. Figure 11 projects SCOUT-30K training samples and Anchor-400 into a shared per-category UMAP. Anchors cover every category, and the per-category anchor count scales with training mass, so denser regions such as hidden_tricky and aligned_instruction receive proportionally more anchors. The same diagnostic gives similar coverage patterns for carrier type, attack type, and hiding strategy. Figure 12 expands hidden_tricky, the largest attack category, into its ten concealment strategies and shows Anchor-400’s coverage of each.

Appendix C Fingerprint construction and retrieval

This appendix expands Section 3: per-anchor fingerprint construction, asymmetric kNN retrieval, and the trust prior used at inference.

Per-(anchor, detector) record.

For every anchor a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A} and every detector D∈𝒟D\in\mathcal{D}, we run DD on aa once and record the raw outputs y^D​(a)∈{0,1}\hat{y}_{D}(a)\in\{0,1\}, latency ℓD​(a)\ell_{D}(a), and confidence cD​(a)c_{D}(a). We then assemble a structured sample context

ctx(a,d)={\displaystyle\text{ctx}(a,d)=\bigl\{ anchor metadata,eval_content,\displaystyle\text{anchor metadata},\;\text{eval\_content},
policy/goal,y^D​(a),y⁡(a),\displaystyle\text{policy/goal},\;\hat{y}_{D}(a),\;y(a),
vd(a),cD(a),ℓD(a)},\displaystyle v_{d}(a),\;c_{D}(a),\;\ell_{D}(a)\bigr\},

where the verdict label vd​(a)∈{TP,TN,FP,FN}v_{d}(a)\in\{\textsf{TP},\textsf{TN},\textsf{FP},\textsf{FN}\} is derived from y^D​(a)\hat{y}_{D}(a) and the ground truth y⁡(a)y(a). This context plus a hand-crafted one-paragraph detector profile for DD (mechanism description; the same string is reused across all anchors of the same detector) is fed to a strong off-the-shelf LLM (openai/gpt-oss-120b via OpenRouter, batch size 55, temperature 0.20.2). The LLM is instructed to emit a JSON array with three fields per anchor:

  1. 1.

    detector_profile: one sentence describing what DD does and how it works.

  2. 2.

    sample_characteristics: up to three sentences describing the anchor’s content, attack-vs-benign label, category, difficulty, carrier type, attack mechanism, and goal. This is the only retrieval-side text (see below).

  3. 3.

    prediction_result: one sentence stating DD’s verdict, whether it was correct, the confidence, and the latency.

The resulting per-detector JSON is the fingerprint database; |𝒜|×|𝒟||\mathcal{A}|\times|\mathcal{D}| entries total.

Asymmetric retrieval at inference.

We retrieve the top-KK anchors per test sample using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025b) in an asymmetric query/document configuration with K=10K=10. The full top-1010 neighbourhood is used for the trust prior below; the outcome predictor (Appendix D) is conditioned on the 55 nearest of these records. Both sides L2-normalize embeddings; we rank by cosine similarity, which reduces to a dot product:

sim⁡(x,a)\displaystyle\mathrm{sim}(x,a) =⟨eq​(x),ed​(a)⟩,\displaystyle=\;\langle\,e_{q}(x),\;e_{d}(a)\,\rangle,
𝒩K​(x)\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{K}(x) =argtopKa∈𝒜sim⁡(x,a).\displaystyle=\;\mathop{\mathrm{argtopK}}_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\;\mathrm{sim}(x,a).

The query side encodes the raw eval_content of the test sample under a task instruction that explicitly asks the embedder to align on (i) injection category (totally_benign, aligned_instruction, direct_misaligned, hidden_tricky, tool_misuse, exfiltration), (ii) hiding strategy (explicit, paraphrased, encoded, context-switching, structurally camouflaged), (iii) carrier type (plain text, code, email, HTML, markdown, tool output / description, table, QA context), and (iv) attack mechanism, while disregarding the topical subject matter of the carrier. The document side encodes each anchor’s sample_characteristics string under a matching instruction asking the embedder to represent the record along the same four dimensions.

Retrieval is detector-agnostic: neither side sees detector identity, and sample_characteristics describes only the anchor sample. A single anchor index serves every detector in the pool. We use D3D_{3}_deberta’s fingerprints to source the document strings; any detector’s sample_characteristics would yield the same retrieval because the field is detector-agnostic. Both sides cache embeddings to disk, so adding a detector reuses the existing index.

Descriptor space coverage.

Figure 13 projects the fingerprint descriptors onto a UMAP and colors them by attack category, carrier type, and difficulty. The descriptors organize by injection structure (category, carrier, and difficulty), which is what the asymmetric retrieval relies on: an incoming request is matched to anchors that share its category, carrier, and difficulty, so the retrieved fingerprints report behavior on structurally similar inputs.

Retrieval quality.

The trust prior and retrieved context are useful when the top-KK anchors share the query’s injection type, since detector behavior tracks attack type. Figure 14 measures attack-type retrieval on SCOUT-450. The top-1010 neighbourhood contains a same-attack_type anchor for 81%81\% of queries overall (67%67\% on attacks, 99%99\% on benign; panel a). Coverage is high for the well-populated types (benign .99.99, instruction_override .93.93, tool_misuse .71.71, credential_exfiltration .70.70) and lower for the three rarest attack types (parameter_manipulation, task_hijacking, retrieval_redirection, each with n≤30n\leq 30 anchors), tracking anchor mass (panel b). Panel (c) shows the fingerprint compaction: each anchor record is ∼\sim69 tokens versus ∼\sim535 for its raw content, an 87%87\% reduction that keeps the predictor’s KK-shot context small.

Why compact records.

The serialization lets the outcome predictor condition on retrieved behavior cheaply: it reads the KK nearest sample_characteristics records in-context (Appendix D), and these compact records hold that context to a few hundred tokens, well under the thousands the corresponding raw eval_content would require (Figure 14c). The serialization runs once, offline, over the fixed anchor bank and is never repeated per request; at inference the only retrieval-side cost is embedding the incoming request, which is passed to the predictor as raw content.

Trust prior at inference.

Given the top-KK anchors 𝒩K​(x)\mathcal{N}_{K}(x) and the per-anchor real correctness labels 𝟏[y^D(a)=y(a)]\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{D}(a)=y(a)] (already computed when building the fingerprint database), the per-sample kNN trust for detector DD on test sample xx is the empirical accuracy of DD on the retrieved neighborhood:

πx,D=1K∑a∈𝒩K​(x)[y^D(a)=y(a)],\pi_{x,D}\;=\;\frac{1}{K}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{N}_{K}(x)}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{D}(a)=y(a)\right], (6)

which lies in [0,1][0,1]. We additionally precompute a global per-detector reliability term, the accuracy of DD over the entire anchor set 𝒜\mathcal{A},

π¯D=1|𝒜|∑a∈𝒜[y^D(a)=y(a)],\bar{\pi}_{D}\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\hat{y}_{D}(a)=y(a)\right], (7)

which is computed once, offline, and uses no test data. The routing rule then applies the effective trust

π~x,D=ω​πx,D+(1−ω)​π¯D,ω∈[0,1],\widetilde{\pi}_{x,D}\;=\;\omega\,\pi_{x,D}+(1-\omega)\,\bar{\pi}_{D},\quad\omega\in[0,1], (8)

in the routing rule (Section 5). The mixing weight ω\omega trades a per-sample local signal (ω→1\omega\to 1) against a global per-detector signal (ω→0\omega\to 0); we use ω=0.6\omega=0.6 by default and report the full sweep in Appendix F. Anchor-side latency ℓ¯D​(x)=(1/K)​∑a∈𝒩K​(x)ℓD​(a)\bar{\ell}_{D}(x)=(1/K)\sum_{a\in\mathcal{N}_{K}(x)}\ell_{D}(a) is computed analogously and surfaced to the predictor as a side feature.

Adding a new detector.

Plugging detector D′D^{\prime} into SCOUT requires three steps: (1) run D′D^{\prime} once on every anchor and store (y^D′​(a),ℓD′​(a),cD′​(a))(\hat{y}_{D^{\prime}}(a),\ell_{D^{\prime}}(a),c_{D^{\prime}}(a)); (2) write a one-paragraph detector profile for D′D^{\prime} and call the fingerprint LLM once per batch of 55 anchors to produce the JSON records; (3) optionally precompute π¯D′\bar{\pi}_{D^{\prime}}. The retrieval index, the embedder, the predictor, and the routing rule are unchanged. This is the integration overhead behind the pool-extension experiments in Section 7.4.

Appendix D Predictor training details

This appendix expands the two-stage recipe of Section 4: hindsight SFT followed by GRPO. We describe what each stage optimizes and why, with the training frameworks and full hyperparameters given below.

Stage 1: hindsight SFT.

The SFT stage trains the predictor on the SCOUT-30K corpus to produce, for every (sample, detector) pair (x,D)(x,D), an assistant turn of the form “zz ∥\| Predicted Performance: {correctness, latency}”, where zz is a short justification and the JSON suffix is the structured prediction. Targets are constructed by hindsight distillation: a teacher LLM is shown the prompt P⁡(x,D)P(x,D), the detector verdict y^D​(x)\hat{y}_{D}(x), the gold label y⁡(x)y(x), and latency ℓD​(x)\ell_{D}(x), then asked to justify the target (𝟏[y^D(x)=y(x)],ℓD(x))(\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{D}(x)=y(x)],\ell_{D}(x)). The teacher’s output is parsed into (z,pred_corr,pred_lat)(z,\texttt{pred\_corr},\texttt{pred\_lat}), and we retain only pairs whose prediction matches that target, yielding the 29,55129{,}551 kept examples that make up SCOUT-30K. Thus pred_corr is a correctness forecast, not a forecast of the detector’s attack/benign verdict.

The training objective is the standard token-level cross-entropy on the assistant turn (loss masked over the prompt). We train two variants from the same dataset:

  • •

    SFT-CoT: the full assistant turn z∥z\,\| JSON. The predictor learns to emit a short reasoning chain followed by the structured prediction.

  • •

    SFT-NoCoT: the rationale zz is dropped at training time and the assistant turn is the JSON alone. This isolates how much of the routing signal depends on the model writing a chain of thought before emitting the structured output.

SFT brings the parse-failure rate to zero but does not, on its own, lift pred_corr accuracy on the light pool above the base Qwen3-4B (the predictor-recipe block of Table 2). It learns the output format of a calibrated predictor without yet learning the calibration. SFT-CoT initializes Stage 2; SFT-NoCoT is kept as an ablation point.

Stage 2: GRPO with a gated multiplicative reward.

Stage 2 starts from the SFT-CoT checkpoint and continues training on the same dataset with group-relative policy optimization (Shao et al., 2024). For each prompt P⁡(x,D)P(x,D), the current policy emits a group of GG candidate completions {o1,…,oG}\{o_{1},\dots,o_{G}\}. Each oio_{i} is scored with the reward R⁡(oi,x,D)R(o_{i};x,D) of Equation 4, and the per-sample advantage is the within-group standardization

Ai=Ri−1G​∑jRjstdj​(Rj)+ε,A_{i}\;=\;\frac{R_{i}\;-\;\tfrac{1}{G}\sum_{j}R_{j}}{\mathrm{std}_{j}(R_{j})+\varepsilon}, (9)

which removes the prompt-level baseline without learning a separate value head. The policy is updated with the standard PPO clipped surrogate over {(oi,Ai)}\{(o_{i},A_{i})\} and is anchored to the SFT-CoT initialization by a low-coefficient KL penalty against the frozen reference, which preserves the SFT-acquired output format and rationale style while letting the correctness and latency tokens move under the reward. We do not add an entropy bonus.

The reward R⁡(o,x,D)=gfmt​(o)⋅rcorr​(o)⋅(1+rlat​(o))R(o;x,D)=g_{\text{fmt}}(o)\cdot r_{\text{corr}}(o)\cdot(1+r_{\text{lat}}(o)) has three pieces, all scoped to the assistant turn after stripping any chain-of-thought tags.

  • •

    Format gate gfmt​(o)∈{0,1}g_{\text{fmt}}(o)\in\{0,1\}: composed of two checks. (i) Length gate: responses exceeding a hard length cap are zeroed; this is the verbosity penalty referenced in Section 7.6, and it compresses the SFT-CoT chain from ∼130\sim 130 tokens to ∼110\sim 110 at convergence. (ii) Parse gate: the response must contain a single Predicted Performance block with both correctness ∈{0,1}\in\{0,1\} and a numerically parseable latency. Any failure on (i) or (ii) zeros the entire reward.

  • •

    Correctness reward rcorr∈{0,1}r_{\text{corr}}\in\{0,1\}: binary exact-match between the parsed correctness and 𝟏[y^D(x)=y(x)]\mathbf{1}[\hat{y}_{D}(x)=y(x)]. There is no soft credit; the reward is multiplicative so wrong correctness predictions collapse the latency contribution to zero as well.

  • •

    Latency reward rlat∈[0,1]r_{\text{lat}}\in[0,1]: a plateau-decay function of the predicted-vs-observed latency error Δ=|pred_lat−ℓD​(x)|\Delta=|\texttt{pred\_lat}-\ell_{D}(x)|. With tolerance δ=max⁡(δmin, 0.5​ℓD​(x))\delta=\max(\delta_{\min},\,0.5\,\ell_{D}(x)),

    rlat={1,Δ≤δ/2,(δ−Δ)/(δ/2),δ/2<Δ≤δ,0,Δ>δ.r_{\text{lat}}\;=\;\begin{cases}1,&\Delta\leq\delta/2,\\ (\delta-\Delta)/(\delta/2),&\delta/2<\Delta\leq\delta,\\ 0,&\Delta>\delta.\end{cases}

    Predictions within 25%25\% of ground truth get full credit; credit decays linearly to zero at 50%50\% off (Figure 15). The small absolute floor δmin\delta_{\min} keeps the reward well-defined for very small ℓD​(x)\ell_{D}(x) (rule-based detectors). The multiplicative coupling (1+rlat)(1+r_{\text{lat}}) ensures latency reward only amplifies a correct prediction and never compensates for an incorrect one.

What each piece is doing. The format gate disciplines the rollout distribution so the gradient sees parseable answers; without it, the policy can game the latency reward via verbose hedging. The correctness reward is the routing signal: it aligns pred_corr with whether the detector will match the gold label, closing the light-pool calibration gap that pure SFT cannot (Appendix H, Figure 20). The latency reward provides a secondary, finer signal that is informative only when correctness is satisfied; it calibrates pred_lat against observed detector latency, which is what lets the routing rule predict the wall-clock ℓ^​(x)\hat{\ell}(x) of each decision (Algorithm 1) and lets τ\tau control latency against a predicted budget (Section 7.6, Appendix E). Checkpoint selection is by routing accuracy on a held-out validation slice of the SCOUT-30K-derived RL split; the selected checkpoint is the one used in every experiment that names “SCOUT” in this paper.

Hyperparameters.

Both stages fine-tune Qwen3-4B-Instruct with LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) (rank 128128, α=256\alpha{=}256, dropout 0.050.05, on all linear layers). The SFT stage uses learning rate 2×10−42{\times}10^{-4} (cosine schedule, 0.10.1 warmup ratio), per-device batch size 44 with gradient accumulation 88, sequence length 40964096, for 33 epochs in bf16. The GRPO stage uses the group-relative estimator with G=8G{=}8 rollouts per prompt, train batch size 192192, PPO mini-batch size 6464, actor learning rate 1.5×10−51.5{\times}10^{-5}, and a low-variance KL penalty against the frozen SFT-CoT reference with coefficient 0.0010.001 (applied in the loss, not folded into the reward); we use no entropy bonus and cap responses at 350350 tokens, training for 33 epochs. Checkpoints are saved every 1010 steps and selected by routing accuracy on the held-out RL validation slice (the selected checkpoint is global step 462462). The routing knobs are not learned: the trust-mixing weight ω=0.6\omega{=}0.6 (Appendix F) and the operator threshold τ=0.875\tau{=}0.875 (Section 7.6) are both fixed by the reported sweeps.

Compute budget.

The predictor is a single Qwen3-4B-Instruct (∼\sim4B parameters). All training runs on one A100 80GB GPU. Stage 1 (SFT) takes about 4.54.5 wall-clock hours; Stage 2 (GRPO) takes about 6060 wall-clock hours to run the full checkpoint schedule from which we select. Building the Anchor-400 fingerprint database queries the off-the-shelf fingerprint LLM once per batch of 55 anchors per detector, at roughly 55–1010 s per call depending on API load, for a total of a few hours of API wall-clock; this is a one-time offline cost and is not repeated at inference. Inference-time predictor latency is the measured 2525 ms per request reported in Appendix K.

Implementation and package versions.

Predictor training uses LLaMA-Factory (Zheng et al., 2024) for the SFT stage and veRL (Sheng et al., 2024) for the GRPO stage, both built on HuggingFace Transformers (Wolf et al., 2020); inference is served with vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) batched decoding. Sentence embeddings for the D2D_{2} family and for retrieval use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025b); the D2D_{2} classifiers use scikit-learn (Pedregosa et al., 2011) defaults except for the kk-nearest-neighbors neighborhood size (k=25k{=}25). UMAP (McInnes et al., 2018) projections in the appendix figures use umap-learn with cosine distance, 1515 neighbors, and min_dist=0.1=0.1. We will release exact version pins and configuration files with the code.

Appendix E Triage rule details

This appendix expands Section 5 and walks through Algorithm 1 line by line. The rule converts the predictor’s per-detector estimates into a single verdict for a test sample xx in three stages: subset selection, a trust-weighted vote within the selected subset, and a symmetric escalation gate. The light pool 𝒟light\mathcal{D}_{\text{light}}, the judge DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}, the threshold τ\tau, and the mixing weight ω\omega are the only inputs, and no stage is retrained when a detector is added. Figure 16 summarizes this flow before the line-by-line description.

Subset selection (lines 1–2).

The selector keeps the light detectors the predictor judges reliable on xx, S={D∈𝒟light:pred_corr​(x,D)=1}S=\{D\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{light}}:\texttt{pred\_corr}(x,D)=1\}. This is a hard inclusion test: a detector with pred_corr​(x,D)=0\texttt{pred\_corr}(x,D)=0 is dropped from the vote entirely and contributes no weight. The estimate is binary by design: whether a detector enters SS is a discrete decision, because a detector is either executed on xx or not, and carries a fixed latency when run. The continuous reliability signal is retained separately as the trust prior πx,D∈[0,1]\pi_{x,D}\in[0,1] (Eq. 6), which weights each selected detector’s vote (Eq. 8). Selecting which detectors run and weighting their votes are thus separated on purpose: pred_corr decides which detectors run, and πx,D\pi_{x,D} decides how much each one counts. Selection is where the predictor exerts most of its influence; it is not scaled by ω\omega, which only mixes the vote weights of the detectors already in SS. When S=∅S=\emptyset, no light detector is trusted on xx and the rule returns the judge verdict directly. This empty-subset case is the rule’s built-in fallback: an input far from every anchor drives the retrieved trust evidence down, the predictor estimates no light detector as reliable, and xx is routed to DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} without consulting the threshold τ\tau.

Trust-weighted vote (lines 4–7).

The selected subset runs in parallel and each detector emits a binary verdict y^D​(x)\hat{y}_{D}(x). The verdicts are combined by the effective-trust weights wD=ω​πx,D+(1−ω)​π¯Dw_{D}=\omega\,\pi_{x,D}+(1-\omega)\,\bar{\pi}_{D} of Equation 8, giving the soft vote v=∑D∈SwD​y^D​(x)/∑D∈SwD∈[0,1]v=\sum_{D\in S}w_{D}\,\hat{y}_{D}(x)\,/\,\sum_{D\in S}w_{D}\in[0,1]. The agreement max⁡(v, 1−v)\max(v,\,1-v) measures how decisively the subset leans toward one label. When agreement reaches the threshold τ\tau, the rule short-circuits and returns 𝟏[v>0.5]\mathbf{1}[v>0.5] without running the judge. This is the path that gives SCOUT its latency advantage, since the light subset runs in parallel and the judge call is skipped.

Symmetric escalation gate (lines 9–11).

When agreement falls below τ\tau, the subset vote is uncertain and the rule considers escalating to the judge. Escalation happens only if the same predictor estimates the judge to be reliable on xx, pred_corr​(x,DLLM)=1\texttt{pred\_corr}(x,D_{\text{LLM}})=1; otherwise the rule keeps the subset vote 𝟏[v>0.5]\mathbf{1}[v>0.5]. The gate is symmetric because one predictor scores reliability on both sides: it can both withhold a useful escalation and trigger an unhelpful one, so it is not an oracle that fires only when the judge would be correct. Section 7.3 ablates the selector and the gate separately to attribute the contribution of each.

The threshold τ\tau.

τ\tau is the deployment-time knob of Section 5 (Equation 5): a low τ\tau escalates rarely and stays cheap, a high τ\tau escalates more and approaches the always-judge baseline. Sweeping τ\tau over [0.5,1.0][0.5,1.0] traces the trade-off in Figure 3. We report τ=0.875\tau=0.875, the knee of the SCOUT-450 sweep: it attains the lowest ASR and the highest Acc, and beyond it more escalation only adds latency (Figure 23) without improving ASR, BU, or Acc (Figure 3). We use this single operating point for the SCOUT row, the ablations of Section 7.3, and the appendix tables.

Deployment recipe for τ\tau.

At deployment, the operator picks τ\tau by running SCOUT once on a small labeled slice of the target traffic and sweeping τ\tau to trace the local safety–utility frontier (Figure 3 shows this trace on SCOUT-450). The operator then selects τ\tau to meet a stated budget: a latency budget LL via Equation 5, which is label-free because T^​(τ)\hat{T}(\tau) comes from pred_lat (Figure 17); a safety target, which needs the labeled slice to measure ASR; or an LLM-call budget through the empirical escalation rate ρ⁡(τ)=|{x:rule escalates on ​x}|/|X|\rho(\tau)=|\{x:\text{rule escalates on }x\}|/|X|, observable from server logs with no labels. The selected τ\tau is frozen for production. The operator monitors live ρ\rho as a cheap drift signal: a sustained shift away from the calibration value triggers a re-sweep on a fresh labeled batch. When labeled validation data is unavailable at deployment, SCOUT ships with τ=0.875\tau=0.875 (the SCOUT-450 headline) as the default.

Selecting τ\tau from a budget.

Both budget readings invert a monotone sweep. Because the LLM judge dominates per-request wall-clock (Appendix K), the escalation rate ρ⁡(τ)\rho(\tau) sets the cost, and ρ\rho increases monotonically with τ\tau (Figure 18); the predicted total T^​(τ)=∑xℓ^​(x)\hat{T}(\tau)=\sum_{x}\hat{\ell}(x) therefore also increases monotonically with τ\tau, where ℓ^​(x)\hat{\ell}(x) is the per-request predicted wall-clock returned by Algorithm 1 from pred_lat. The attack block rate 1−ASR⁡(τ)1-\mathrm{ASR}(\tau) rises with τ\tau up to the headline operating point and then plateaus. The operator thus reads the threshold off whichever budget is binding: a latency budget LL gives τ⋆​(L)=max⁡{τ:T^​(τ)≤L}\tau^{\star}(L)=\max\{\tau:\hat{T}(\tau)\leq L\} (the safest threshold affordable under LL), and a safety budget qq gives τ⋆​(q)=min⁡{τ:1−ASR⁡(τ)≥q}\tau^{\star}(q)=\min\{\tau:1-\mathrm{ASR}(\tau)\geq q\} (the cheapest threshold meeting qq). The latency reading is more feasible because the predictor estimates pred_lat, so the wall-clock of a candidate τ\tau is known before any request runs. Figure 17 plots both maps on SCOUT-450; the headline τ=0.875\tau=0.875 lies on both curves.

Detector-invocation portfolio across the τ\tau-sweep.

Figure 18 visualizes how the routed system allocates its detector budget on SCOUT-450 as τ\tau sweeps the operating frontier (rows: candidate LLM judges; columns: the three τ\tau values from Table 1 plus τ=1.00\tau{=}1.00 as the upper bound). For each request we count detector invocations: every light detector that voted, plus DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} on every escalated request. Each panel annotates the empirical escalation rate ρ⁡(τ)\rho(\tau).

The pies trace the empirical ρ⁡(τ)\rho(\tau): as τ\tau rises, the share of requests escalated to DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} grows monotonically and saturates near 60%60\% at the headline operating point (the under-100%100\% plateau at τ=1.00\tau{=}1.00 reflects the symmetric escalation gate, which withholds the judge whenever the predictor estimates it unreliable on the input). Within-light-pool composition stays essentially constant across τ\tau and across both judges, so τ\tau works as an escalation-budget knob with little effect on which light detectors get used.

Per-path latency.

The easy path costs one batched predictor call plus the parallel execution of SS, so its detector latency is the maximum over the selected subset, because the detectors run in parallel. The escalated path additionally pays the sequential judge call. The full deployment model, the measured predictor wall-clock, and the per-path breakdown are given in Appendix K; the sensitivity to ω\omega is in Appendix F.
