Appendix H Per-predictor quality

This appendix supports the predictor-recipe ablation in Section 7.3 with two views of predictor quality on SCOUT-450.

Per-predictor pred_corr quality and verbosity.

Figure 20 shows per-predictor pred_corr accuracy (left) and mean output tokens (right). On the light pool, SCOUT leads at .74.74, ahead of the SFT and base variants at .58.58–.66.66 (Table 6); this gap orders the predictor recipes in Table 2. On the more accurate DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} judge the spread narrows, with SCOUT at .93.93 and the other recipes between .84.84 and .92.92, so the differentiator at the routing layer is light-pool calibration. SFT alone calibrates the output format (parse-failure rate drops to zero) but does not improve the underlying signal; the second-stage RL fine-tuning (Section 4) with an exact-match correctness reward raises calibrated accuracy on the light pool. SCOUT is also the second-most concise predictor: the reward’s length gate (Equation 4) compresses chain-of-thought from ∼130\sim 130 tokens (SFT-CoT) to ∼110\sim 110, leaving only the no-CoT baseline shorter.

Predictor comparison, including non-LLM baselines.

Table 6 compares every predictor by raw pred_corr accuracy on SCOUT-450, broken out by detector group. Alongside the LLM-predictor recipes we add two non-LLM predictor baselines that replace the Qwen3-4B model but leave SCOUT’s routing rule unchanged: KNN predicts each detector’s correctness as the majority outcome over the 1010 nearest Anchor-400 samples (cosine over Qwen3-Embedding), and MLP is a two-layer network over the sample embedding concatenated with a detector one-hot, trained on the Anchor-400 (sample, detector) pairs. SCOUT is the most accurate predictor on every detector group, and the margin is largest on the light pool, which is the group that governs the routing trade-off position (Table 2). The non-LLM baselines remain weakly calibrated on the light pool (.63.63–.68.68 against SCOUT’s .74.74), and their routing outcomes appear in the predictor-recipe block of Table 2. Two comparisons within the LLM-predictor family isolate SCOUT’s design choices. First, the reasoning chain helps: the SFT-CoT recipe reaches .639.639 light-pool predicted-correctness accuracy against .577.577 for the bare-JSON SFT-NoCoT recipe, and the GRPO stage is built on the CoT variant, so the chain-of-thought carries task signal beyond output formatting. Second, the retrieved fingerprints help: with chain-of-thought held fixed on the base predictor, supplying the top-55 fingerprints (5-shot) over no context (0-shot) raises predicted-correctness accuracy from .649.649 to .655.655 on the light pool and from .674.674 to .681.681 overall. This gain is small but consistent; the stronger evidence that retrieval surfaces the right history is the coverage and alignment analysis in Appendix C.

Appendix I Predictor as a standalone detector

For diagnostics, we evaluate the SCOUT predictor as a standalone binary detector. It emits an attack/benign verdict directly from the same SFT++GRPO checkpoint used inside SCOUT, without the fingerprint database, trust prior, or routing rule. The model is served via vLLM with the same prompt template as DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} and the same GRPO LoRA (global step 462462) merged into the SFT-CoT base. Table 7 reports the results.

On the in-distribution SCOUT-450 split, the standalone direct-detector prompt matches the always-judge baseline within 0.30.3 accuracy points (.927.927 vs. .924.924). Wall-clock per request drops to ∼11\sim 11 ms, versus ∼1500\sim 1500 ms for the API-backed DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}, because local batched vLLM serving amortizes the checkpoint over a GPU batch. This direct-detector measurement differs from SCOUT’s routing predictor call in Appendix K, which runs one detector-profile prompt for each member of the light pool and the judge and costs 2525 ms per request at batch size 88. We do not claim the predictor is “cheap” in absolute compute terms. On the three external OOD benchmarks, recall collapses to .25.25–.46.46, mostly from missed hidden_tricky and direct_misaligned attacks. Precision remains high (≥.74\geq.74), so the failures are silent attack passes, with few benign false alarms.

These results motivate SCOUT’s use as an orchestration layer. The predictor inherits the distributional bias of SCOUT-30K, which limits standalone deployment outside the training distribution. SCOUT recovers usable behavior on these benchmarks (Section 7, Table 4) by selecting among detectors with different failure modes, so its out-of-distribution robustness comes from the detector pool and the routing rule.

Appendix J Extended generalization study

External benchmarks.

We evaluate on a 1,0001{,}000-sample slice of each of three external benchmarks. BIPIA (Yi et al., 2025) is an indirect-prompt-injection benchmark over five LLM-integrated tasks (email, web, table, and code question answering, and summarization), with malicious instructions embedded in the external content; it defines 3030 text and 3030 code attack types grouped into task-irrelevant, task-relevant, and targeted categories. Our slice is de-duplicated and disjoint from every BIPIA example SCOUT uses (Section 7.5). IPI (Wen et al., 2025) follows the indirect-prompt-injection setup of the InstructDetector study, with injected instructions placed in retrieved external documents. IHEval (Zhang et al., 2025c) evaluates instruction-hierarchy following: it contains 3,5383{,}538 examples over nine tasks in four scenarios (rule following, task execution, safety defense, tool use), each with aligned and conflicting instructions across system messages, user messages, conversation history, and tool outputs; we map hierarchy-conflicting cases to attacks and aligned cases to benign. The three differ in attack style and structure, which is why the strongest detector changes across them (Table 8).

This appendix supports Tables 3–4 with two latency-vs-quality views: pool extensions under the two LLM judges (Figure 21) and external benchmarks (Figure 22). The standalone per-detector reference on SCOUT-450 is read off the single-detector rows of Table 1.

Per-detector breakdown on the external benchmarks.

Table 8 expands Table 4 with the per-detector results on BIPIA, IPI, and IHEval (N=1000N{=}1000 each) under both judges. Single-detector rows are independent of the judge choice; the Always-DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} and SCOUT rows match the corresponding rows of Table 4.

Three observations follow.

The strongest single detector shifts across benchmarks, and on BIPIA it is not the LLM judge. On BIPIA, D3D_{3} (Acc .932.932) and D8D_{8} (Acc .928.928) both outperform the GPT-5.1 judge (Acc .873.873) at a fraction of its wall-clock; D9D_{9} reaches lower ASR but pays a large BU cost. On IPI the judge wins by a clear margin. On IHEval, light-detector quality collapses (most non-degenerate detectors fall below .55.55 Acc), and D4D_{4}, degenerate on the other two benchmarks, becomes the strongest light detector. No fixed light detector covers all three benchmarks.

SCOUT’s allocation extracts the benchmark-specific strengths. On BIPIA, SCOUT reaches the highest Acc while keeping ASR close to the best high-recall detector and BU close to the judge. On IPI, SCOUT matches the judge on Acc and keeps ASR near the best light-detector value without inheriting that detector’s BU collapse. On IHEval, where the light pool is mostly non-discriminative, SCOUT keeps BU above .70.70 under both judges; with GPT-5.1 it also keeps ASR below .10.10, whereas the GPT-4o run trades that safety target for higher BU and lower wall-clock.

The wall-clock budget reflects this allocation. SCOUT cuts the GPT-5.1 judge’s wall-clock by 3.7×3.7\times on BIPIA, 1.4×1.4\times on IPI, and 1.2×1.2\times on IHEval; the cut tracks how often the predictor can route to a reliable light detector. On IHEval, where light coverage is thin, escalation is almost mandatory and the wall-clock saving is the smallest.

Appendix K End-to-end deployment study

This appendix backs the latency numbers in Table 1 and Section 7.6 with the deployment model, the per-predictor end-to-end breakdown, and the break-even derivation.

Deployment model.

End-to-end wall-clock per request decomposes as T⁡(x)=Tpred​(x)+Tdetect​(x)T(x)=T_{\text{pred}}(x)+T_{\text{detect}}(x). The predictor runs once per request as a single batched call of size |𝒟light∪{DLLM}|=8|\mathcal{D}_{\text{light}}\!\cup\!\{D_{\text{LLM}}\}|=8, one prompt per detector profile against the same target sample; the routing rule then runs the filtered light pool in parallel and, when the rule decides to escalate, makes a sequential call to the LLM judge DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}. TdetectT_{\text{detect}} is read directly from each row’s routing column (Table 2); TpredT_{\text{pred}} is reported below.

Predictor wall-clock.

We measure TpredT_{\text{pred}} for the SCOUT predictor on a single A100 80GB under vLLM batched decoding: 2525 ms per request at batch size 88 across the predictor’s typical ∼110\sim 110 output tokens. For the other predictor recipes we scale linearly by mean output length (verbosity is the dominant factor on memory-bandwidth-bound decode), giving the TpredT_{\text{pred}} column of Table 9.

Findings.

Table 9 reports each recipe’s predictor (TpredT_{\text{pred}}) and detector (TdetectT_{\text{detect}}) wall-clock and the total. Two points stand out. (i) Predictor verbosity dominates the gap between predictor recipes. A 5-shot base predictor emits ∼720\sim 720 tokens on average and a 0-shot base predictor still emits ∼510\sim 510, so their predictor wall-clock alone is 0.120.12–0.170.17 s; SFT-CoT compresses chain-of-thought to ∼130\sim 130 tokens, and SCOUT (via the reward’s length gate, Equation 4) further down to ∼110\sim 110 tokens and the measured 2525 ms. (ii) SCOUT is the only configuration to exceed always-judge accuracy at lower latency. SCOUT lands at 0.880.88 s (−40%-40\% vs. the 1.461.46 s baseline) and .933.933 accuracy (+0.9+0.9 pts above always-judge); the other recipes either trail on accuracy or pay more on the predictor wall-clock for the same latency budget.

Break-even derivation (Section 7.6).

SCOUT replaces every DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} call with a predictor call. A fraction pescp_{\text{esc}} of requests then escalates to DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}; the remaining 1−pesc1-p_{\text{esc}} finish on the filtered light pool at latency TlightT_{\text{light}} (parallel-max over the filtered subset). End-to-end per request is

TSCOUT=Tpred+(1−pesc)​Tlight+pesc​TDLLM.T_{\text{SCOUT}}\;=\;T_{\text{pred}}+(1-p_{\text{esc}})\,T_{\text{light}}+p_{\text{esc}}\,T_{D_{\text{LLM}}}.

SCOUT is faster than always-judge (TSCOUT<TDLLMT_{\text{SCOUT}}<T_{D_{\text{LLM}}}) iff

(1−pesc)​(TDLLM−Tlight)>Tpred.(1-p_{\text{esc}})(T_{D_{\text{LLM}}}-T_{\text{light}})>T_{\text{pred}}.

The left side is the average judge latency saved by short-circuiting; the right side is the predictor overhead paid on every request. At our measured operating point (Tpred=0.025T_{\text{pred}}=0.025 s, TDLLM=1.457T_{D_{\text{LLM}}}=1.457 s, pesc=256/450=0.569p_{\text{esc}}=256/450=0.569), the routing column Tdetect=0.853T_{\text{detect}}=0.853 s implies Tlight≈0.062T_{\text{light}}\approx 0.062 s (the per-sample max-light at median per-detector latency is dominated by D5D_{5}_align_sentinel at ∼58\sim 58 ms). The saved-judge term is (194/450)​(1.457−0.062)≈0.601(194/450)(1.457-0.062)\approx 0.601 s, well above the 0.0250.025 s predictor overhead. Plugging back in gives TSCOUT=0.025+0.853=0.878T_{\text{SCOUT}}=0.025+0.853=0.878 s <1.457<1.457 s, matching the Table 9 total up to rounding.

Predicted vs realized wall-clock.

Because the predictor estimates pred_lat, SCOUT predicts the total wall-clock T^​(τ)\hat{T}(\tau) of its own routing before any request runs. Figure 23 plots T^​(τ)\hat{T}(\tau) against the realized total across the τ\tau-sweep on SCOUT-450 and the three external benchmarks. On SCOUT-450 the curves match in magnitude (mean gap 2.5%2.5\%); on the external benchmarks the predictor underestimates absolute wall-clock (by up to 29%29\% on the slowest cell), because their judges and longer inputs run slower than the SCOUT-30K profiles pred_lat was trained on, but it reproduces the same monotone rise and plateau. The budget-to-τ\tau map (Figure 17) depends only on this monotone trend, so τ\tau selection transfers even where the absolute prediction is biased.

Production considerations.

In Table 9 the LLM-judge and light-detector times are per-request, while the predictor’s wall-clock is an amortized share under batched vLLM serving, where the per-(sample, detector) prompts decode together on the GPU. A production deployment batches the predictor further across concurrent requests, lowering this share still more. We leave a full deployment study to future work: batched-concurrency throughput on benign traffic, a downstream-LLM judging cross-check of pipeline-blocking ASR on samples the router did not flag, and a token-budget comparison against always-LLM-judge and no-defense baselines.

Appendix L LLM judge selection

The main-text experiments use GPT-4o (OpenAI, 2024) as the LLM judge DLLMD_{\text{LLM}}. To choose it, we first ran five candidate judges (GPT-4o, GPT-5.1 (OpenAI, 2026), DeepSeek-V3.2 (DeepSeek-AI, 2025), DeepSeek-V4 (DeepSeek-AI, 2026), and Gemini-3.1 (Google DeepMind, 2026)) on Anchor-400 (Section 6) and selected by accuracy (Table 10). We then evaluated the candidates on the held-out SCOUT-450 benchmark to check whether the Anchor-400 ranking transferred (Table 11). Both protocols use the same prompt template (Section 7.1, eval-only mode), with one query per judge per sample.

Restricted to the judges evaluated on both sets, the two rankings agree (GPT-4o >> GPT-5.1 ≈\approx DeepSeek-V4, with Gemini-3.1 weakest), supporting Anchor-400 as a judge-selection proxy without using the test set. Two judges appear in only one table: DeepSeek-V3.2 was screened out at the Anchor-400 stage and was not re-evaluated on SCOUT-450; GPT-5.2 (OpenAI, 2025b) was added to the candidate set after the initial Anchor-400 screening, as a higher-recall variant, and run only on SCOUT-450. We include GPT-5.2 because it shows a separate operating point, with the lowest ASR in Table 11 but a 0.3850.385 FPR, i.e. flagging 38.5%38.5\% of benign requests. The latency column is API-bound and varies by an order of magnitude across providers, so screening prioritizes accuracy and uses latency only as a tiebreaker.

Appendix N Reproducibility and responsible use

Single-run reporting.

All reported numbers are single runs on fixed held-out sets, without multi-seed variance or confidence intervals. The non-judge components are deterministic (fixed-weight detectors, greedy predictor decoding, and fixed Anchor-400 retrieval), so the only stochastic element is the hosted LLM judge; per-request latency is reported as the median (Appendix K). The τ\tau-sweeps in Section 7 trace the operating curve, so the headline point is the knee of a smooth sweep.

Potential risks.

Releasing SCOUT-450 and the attack-category schema could in principle help an attacker study which prompt-injection structures evade specific detectors. We judge this risk to be low: the attack templates we use are standard instruction-override and exfiltration patterns already present in public benchmarks such as BIPIA, IPI, and IHEval, and SCOUT adds no new attack capability. The released artifacts are intended to advance defense research, and our framework is a defensive orchestration layer.

Use of AI assistants.

Several pipeline components are LLMs by design: an off-the-shelf model (GPT-OSS-120B (OpenAI, 2025a)) serializes detector behavior into fingerprint records (Section 3); a teacher LLM produces the hindsight-distilled rationales that supervise SCOUT-30K (Section 4, Appendix D); the outcome predictor is a fine-tuned Qwen3-4B-Instruct (Section 4); and GPT-4o, with GPT-5.1 as an alternate, serves as the LLM judge DLLMD_{\text{LLM}} (Section 7.1, Appendix L). Separately, during manuscript preparation the authors used a general-purpose AI assistant for language editing and for drafting and debugging plotting and analysis code; all technical claims, experimental design, and analyses were produced and verified by the authors.

Appendix O Licenses and intended use

Artifacts we use.

We use the following external artifacts under their published terms, all for research purposes consistent with their intended use. Benchmarks: BIPIA (Yi et al., 2025), IPI/InstructDetector (Wen et al., 2025), and IHEval (Zhang et al., 2025c) are released for prompt-injection research. Detector backbones and methods: the DeBERTa-v3 prompt-injection classifier (ProtectAI, 2023), DistilBERT indirect-injection classifier (Chen et al., 2025a), AlignSentinel (Jia et al., 2026), Attention Tracker (Hung et al., 2025), and PIGuard (Li et al., 2025a) are used under their respective licenses (we train the D2D_{2}/D3D_{3}/D5D_{5}/D7D_{7}/D8D_{8} weights on our detector training set; D9D_{9} uses the released PIGuard model). Base models: Qwen3-4B-Instruct (Qwen Team, 2025) and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025b) (Apache-2.0/Tongyi terms) and GPT-OSS-120B for fingerprint serialization. The LLM judges (GPT-4o, GPT-5.1) are accessed through their commercial APIs under the providers’ terms of service. Our use of each artifact is limited to research evaluation and is consistent with the access conditions under which it was released.

Artifacts we release.

We release SCOUT-450, Anchor-400, and SCOUT-30K (data), the SFT++GRPO predictor checkpoint (model), the per-detector outputs, and the routing code. The datasets are released for research use only under a CC BY 4.0 license; the predictor checkpoint inherits the Qwen3 base-model terms; the routing and analysis code is released under the MIT license. Because the data was assembled for research on prompt-injection defense, derivatives should remain within research contexts and should not be repurposed to develop or deploy prompt-injection attacks.
